prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat electronic bands in twisted bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states at the magic angle, establishing moire quantum materials

statement.case_for: I keep magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (B017) as my preferred single-part prize. The round-1 exchange did not dispute any fact I rely on: Bistritzer and MacDonald predicted flat bands at a specific twist angle from a continuum model, Jarillo-Herrero's group showed that this regime hosts correlated insulators and superconductivity, and independent groups have reproduced the phases for about eight years. This fits the criterion I quoted in March, a discovery or invention with identifiable originators, since here the originators are a prediction and an experiment that fall to three named people. The consequence is a platform in which twist and stacking geometry, an interface parameter I know well from electron microscopy of oxide and layered interfaces, becomes a control knob for electronic phases. I draw the citation on the existence of the flat bands and the correlated phases, and not on the pairing mechanism, which answers the chair's question and the concern raised by Eriksson and Lindroth. I do not accept that an open pairing mechanism is a maturity problem for this citation: what is credited is the prediction and the observation of the phases, and both are settled.
statement.case_against: I move closer to the majority on the weighing, though not on the facts. Optical lattice clocks (B041) have the cleanest allocation on the list, with six members preferring them and every supporter naming Katori and Ye, and the independently confirmed 1e-18 uncertainties settle maturity. Against that, B017 has a real weakness that no citation fully repairs: Cao and Fatemi, who carried out the 2018 measurements, the Dean, Young and Kim groups on the hBN moire, and earlier twisted-bilayer theory by Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto are outside the three names, and the superconducting phase is still not understood. I cannot claim B017 is the safer prize, only the one I judge to be the more important physics. If the committee decides that maturity and clean attribution should decide, I would vote for B041 without reservation as my second choice, and I would not treat that outcome as a failure of the process.

responses.point: Kroll holds that the interpretation of twisted bilayer graphene is not yet stable, that the pairing mechanism is debated and sample variability is large, and that he would not put B017 ahead of a settled, independently reproduced result such as the lattice clock.
responses.response: The point on the mechanism is correct, but I think it tests the wrong thing. The citation I propose does not say why the material superconducts; it credits a prediction of flat bands and the observation of correlated insulating and superconducting phases at the predicted angle, and those observations have survived many laboratories. Sample variability concerns the quantitative phase diagram, not the existence of the phases. Where I accept your argument is on the comparison of risk: B041 is the lower-risk allocation, and I will say so in my vote ranking. I also note that the boundary you draw for the lattice clock against the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize, tightly around the magic-wavelength lattice, is the right wording if B041 prevails, and I would support it.

responses.point: Lindroth accepts the originality of B017 but says the origin of the superconductivity and sample dependence remain open, that a three-name prize cannot repair the omission of Cao, Fatemi and the hBN moire work, and that she would not oppose it in a year or two.
responses.response: I take the Cao and Fatemi point seriously and it is the strongest argument against my own preference; I have no way to include them under the three-name rule, so the citation should speak of the prediction and the experimental discovery of the phases and not of a list of who measured what. Your suggestion that waiting a year or two costs little is where we differ: the physics will not change for the three named people, and the prize concerns the original work, not the mechanism. I still hear a real maturity concern, and it is the reason that B041 is my first alternative and not a distant one. If you and others judge that the superconducting origin must be known first, tell me what observation would count as sufficient, because I do not think the pairing question will be settled on the timescale of a vote.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, says eight years is short, the superconductivity origin is open and Cao is not on the supplied credit, so he keeps B017 as an alternative and would support it more readily in a few years if a pairing mechanism emerges.
responses.response: Your distinction between a clean prediction and a sharp experiment with named originators is the argument I would build on, and I appreciate that you concede the attribution is better than for IceCube. On timing, waiting for a pairing mechanism makes the prize depend on a later question than the one the prize answers, and I recall earlier condensed-matter prizes awarded before the microscopic explanation was complete, though I have not checked each case here. I accept that eight years is short compared with the clock programme. I do not see IceCube as a competing leader and would not move toward B029 on the present evidence, because the credit among Halzen, Karle, Yoshida and a large collaboration remains the unresolved point you yourself raised.

responses.point: Mehlig calls B017 the most serious rival to the clock, but says the unresolved pairing mechanism and the priority of earlier twisted-bilayer theory by Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto weigh against it, while saying he would not oppose B017 if the committee rewards the platform rather than the mechanism.
responses.response: That is the framing I would adopt: the platform and the observed phases, not the mechanism. On the earlier theory, Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto computed the band structure of twisted bilayers at commensurate angles, but the prediction of exactly flat bands at a magic angle and the argument that this would favour correlated states are what Bistritzer and MacDonald supplied, and that is what the experiment then tested. I would let the citation say prediction of flat bands, not first twisted bilayer calculation. This is a judgement call on priority and I do not claim it is free of dispute.

responses.point: Eriksson shares my reading of the attribution and timing, but says the credit gap includes Cao and Fatemi as well as Dean and Young, that the supplied trio is not exhaustive, and that he would accept B041 prevailing if maturity is judged decisive.
responses.response: I agree that the trio is not exhaustive, and I should not have described the gap in round 1 mainly as Dean and Young. We are in the same position: we prefer B017 on scientific grounds, we treat the three-person limit as its cost, and we both regard B041 as a legitimate outcome. The chair asks whether we would accept B041; yes, I would, and I think we should say that openly. Your interest in B019 does not change my view for this year, since no other member has supported it and the priority and materials questions you recorded are open.

uncertainties: Whether a majority will treat the unresolved pairing mechanism and sample dependence as a reason to wait, or accept a citation limited to the prediction and the observed phases.
Whether Cao, Fatemi and the earlier twisted-bilayer theorists leave the B017 credit too contestable once a three-name limit is applied.

Whether the lattice-clock step in B041 is distinct enough from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, and how much of Ye's credit rests on the lattice clock itself; I rely on colleagues' judgement in atomic physics here.
Whether the committee should wait for a redefinition of the second before awarding B041; I do not think it should, but it is not my field.
statement.conflict_note: No change to my round-1 disclosure. I have Chalmers ties, including committee member Goran Johansson, who prefers B041, and academic exchanges in Japan, where Katori and Miyazaki work. I have no documented personal or institutional relationship with any credited person in B017 or B041 and see no need for recusal; I would flag one if it emerged.
